query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Using a high‐entropy metal diboride synthesis via optimized powder processing and sintering to form a single-phase (e.g., (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2) will allow fabrication at lower temperatures while simultaneously enhancing the material’s hardness, oxidation resistance, and liquid-metal corrosion resistance compared to conventional high-temperature single‐phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requiring >2300 °C for synthesis and previously reported lower‐temperature specimens that exhibit poor oxidation durability and liquid plating-metal corrosion resistance.
generation.intervention: Implement high-entropy metal diboride synthesis via powder processing (using a blend of transition metal powders such as Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, and Ta with boron) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at reduced temperatures (around 1700–1800 °C) to achieve a single-phase high-entropy diboride.
generation.conditions: Powder processing with homogeneously mixed elemental powders, sintered via SPS at reduced temperatures; subsequent evaluation under oxidation testing in flowing dry air up to 1500 °C and exposure to liquid plating-metal environments at service-relevant temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a homogeneous single-phase high-entropy diboride microstructure with refined grain boundaries and reduced porosity, which enhances diffusion-assisted densification and mechanical interlocking.
generation.mechanism: The multi-element (high-entropy) approach increases the configurational entropy, stabilizing the single-phase structure at lower processing temperatures. This dense microstructure, enhanced by liquid-phase–assisted densification during SPS, strengthens covalent bonding across Zr–B and B–B networks, leading to improved hardness and oxidation/corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-entropy metal diboride is expected to be sintered at temperatures near 1700–1800 °C, exhibiting higher hardness, lower oxidation-induced degradation at 1500 °C, and superior resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion compared to conventional ZrB2 fabricated above 2300 °C and previous lower-temperature specimens.
generation.baseline: Benchmark data for conventional single-phase ZrB2 produced at >2300 °C and lower-temperature specimens which show significant oxidation degradation and liquid-metal corrosion.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable in manufacturing settings that utilize powder processing and SPS with maximum processing temperatures of about 1700–1800 °C, and for service environments where the material is exposed to oxidation in dry air up to 1500 °C and continuous liquid plating-metal contact (e.g., in corrosive metal baths).
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative improvements in hardness and oxidation/corrosion resistance are expected, the precise quantitative performance enhancements depend on the exact powder composition, sintering parameters, and post-processing conditions, which require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of high-entropy metal diboride specimens (e.g., (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2) using the proposed powder processing and SPS regime at 1700–1800 °C. In parallel, prepare conventional ZrB2 specimens using the high-temperature (>2300 °C) method and include previously reported lower-temperature specimens. Subject all specimens to identical oxidation tests in flowing dry air at 1500 °C and liquid plating-metal exposure tests. Compare microstructural features using XRD/SEM, Vickers hardness, oxidation weight gains, and corrosion metrics.
measurements: Phase identification and lattice parameter determination by XRD
Microstructural evaluation (grain size, porosity) via SEM/EDS
Hardness testing using a Vickers diamond indenter
Oxidation resistance via weight gain measurements at 1500 °C
Liquid-metal corrosion assessment by measuring weight loss or depth of corrosion attack after predetermined exposure times
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy diboride specimens do not demonstrate a lower sintering temperature (<1800 °C) along with statistically significant improvements in hardness, reduced oxidation weight gain, and enhanced liquid-metal corrosion resistance relative to both conventional ZrB2 and the prior lower-temperature specimens, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To investigate the correlation between the size difference factor (δ) and the phase composition of the samples, we performed XRD analysis on six different high-entropy borides. The results are presented in Figure 2. From the graph, it is evident that (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2 all exhibit a single-phase structure, with their respective lattice parameters listed in Table 1. In contrast, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 show variations. In the XRD patterns of (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 systems, in addition to the high-entropy phase, impurity phases such as (Mo, W)2B5, W2B5, and minor amounts of (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)C and B4C were observed. Notably, these non-single-phase (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 systems corresponded to higher δ values. Hence, it is less likely to form single-phase, high-entropy borides when δ exceeds 3.9%. In the upcoming experiments, our focus will be on (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, which boasts the smallest δ value.

Hardness and oxidation measurements were conducted using all six single-phase high-entropy diborides (HEB #1-#5 and #7) and six individual metal diboride benchmarking specimens (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2) that were made by the same HEBM and SPS fabrication method using the same processing parameters, with one exception that CrB2 was sintered at lower temperature of 1800 °C because its substantially lower melting (and therefore sintering) temperature. MoB2 was not examined because it is not a thermodynamically stable phase (and will decompose to MoB and Mo2B5) below 1500 °C. Hardness measurements were performed with a Vickers’ diamond indenter at 200 kgf/mm2 with a hold time of 15 seconds. The indentations were examined for conformation with the ASTM C1327. The indentations averaged 20–25 μm in width during the testing. Multiple measurements were performed at different locations of each specimen; the mean and standard deviation are reported.
